name: core
description: Fixed ideas, each aimed at one way the dialogue can fail to be verbatim. Change a case only together with a new set name, or old and new runs stop being comparable.

cases.risk: baseline: one speaker, two short sentences
cases.idea: A night gas station in the rain. A girl in a red raincoat slides an envelope to the cashier and says: "You know what is inside. Do not open it until morning."

cases.risk: two speakers, each line must land in its own shot
cases.idea: A rooftop at dawn over a sleeping city. A young man in a grey hoodie tells his sister: "I sold the car. We leave tonight." She smiles and answers: "Then I am driving."

cases.risk: child speaker: voice age, not only gender
cases.idea: A sunny wedding reception on a rooftop. Just as the bride lifts her glass for a toast, a little boy tugs her dress, points at the groom, and loudly says: "That's the man who was crying at my mom's grave yesterday."

cases.risk: numbers and times: models and ASR both like to rewrite them
cases.idea: A crowded airport gate. A tired announcer leans into the microphone and says: "Flight 407 to Lisbon now boards at gate 12, at 9:45."

cases.risk: rare names the model may mispronounce or replace
cases.idea: A hospital corridor at night. A nurse grabs a doctor's sleeve and whispers: "Tell Siobhan that Mr. Kowalczyk woke up."

cases.risk: short contracted words and a dash: easy to drop or expand
cases.idea: A kitchen at 3 a.m. A woman blocks the door and says: "Don't. Not tonight. You can't — not after what he did."

cases.risk: a 25-word line close to the limit of one shot
cases.idea: An empty theatre. An old actor sits on the edge of the stage and says to the last person in the hall: "I have played kings and fools for forty years, and tonight, for the first time, I do not know which one I am."

cases.risk: no quoted line: the script writes the dialogue, so only the script-vs-audio check applies
cases.idea: A lighthouse keeper finds a message in a bottle and reads it aloud to his dog.
